title: My own size
hookLine: take a role beyond your powers and you fail it and neglect the one you could have filled (Enchiridion 37)
carry: the part that really was yours
last: FOR THE SAKE OF THE FELLOWSHIP.

lines: WE HOPED YOU'D CHAIR THE COMMITTEE.
cards: The email says: we were hoping you'd chair the committee. You're flattered. You're also already behind on everything, you've never run a budget, and the committee meets on the night you usually put your kids to bed.
You say yes anyway. Six months later the committee is struggling, and so is bedtime. Section thirty-seven of the handbook is a single sentence, and it names both things that went wrong.

teach.b: If you take on a role beyond your powers, Epictetus says, you disgrace yourself in it, and you neglect the role you could have filled. Two losses, not one. The Greek for role is prosōpon.

It meant a face, then an actor's mask, then the part the mask stood for. Back in section seventeen you met this picture: you're an actor in a play someone else wrote, and your job is to play your part well.

teach.h: TWO LOSSES: THAT ROLE, AND YOURS.
teach.b: Today adds the other side: don't grab a part that isn't yours. Latin used persona for the same idea, mask and role together, and Cicero, drawing on an earlier Stoic, built a whole theory of the roles each person plays.
Now the double cost. The first loss is obvious: the role you weren't ready for goes badly, and people see it. The second is quieter and usually bigger.
The part that really was yours, the friend, the parent, the craftsman, the neighbor, gets the leftovers. Nobody throws a party for a role you neglected. It just thins out.
What this isn't: a rule to stay small forever.
In a couple of weeks the handbook will ask, sharply, how long you're going to wait to become your best. Growth is welcome.
The point is honesty about your present size: what you can carry now, what you're for right now, and which yes would cost a part you've already been given.

how: People practicing Stoicism sometimes review their commitments and decline roles beyond their present powers, to protect the roles they already hold.

o: the script of a play that someone else wrote
a person's private self, hidden behind every role
a face, then a mask, then the role a person plays

games.q: my own size — tap the pairs.
p: the role you could have filled

s: Epictetus says taking on too big a role costs you only that role
two losses: you fail that role, and neglect the one you could have filled.
the Greek word for role first meant a face
prosōpon: face, then the actor's mask, then the part.

games.q: you're asked to chair a committee you can't really carry right now. what does Enchiridion 37 point to?
o: say yes. you'll grow into it.
decline, so you don't fail it and neglect the role you could fill.
say yes, then quietly do nothing.
games.why: a role beyond your powers costs twice: that role goes badly, and the part that was yours gets neglected.

practice: Think of what you've said yes to lately, the invitations, the asks, the jobs you took because nobody else would, and find one that's beyond your powers right now, or keeps eating time from a part that's really yours.
Don't solve it; just name it. Then picture saying, kindly and clearly, I'm not the right person for this, and notice what loosens.

wordCard.voice: Prosōpon. The Greek word for mask, then role; take one beyond your powers and you fail it, and neglect the one you could have filled. Today's word.
